standard_text: Apply the properties of operations (e.g., identity, inverse, commutative, associative, distributive properties) to create equivalent linear expressions, including situations that involve factoring out a common number (e.g., given 2x - 10, create an equivalent expression 2(x - 5)). Justify each step in the process.

progression.narrative: This standard asks students to rewrite a linear expression as an equivalent one by combining like terms, distributing, and factoring out a common number, and to name the property that justifies each step. The on-grade work runs from adding two linear expressions with every sign intact, through naming the property behind a single move, to the core skills of distributing a rational coefficient and factoring to the form p(qx + r). Students who stall here usually carry gaps from well before grade seven: they never internalized that 6 x 14 breaks into 6 x 10 plus 6 x 4, and they cannot read what a phrase or a parenthesis is telling them to do. Intervention should rebuild that grade 3 to 5 base first, then the grade 6 skills of combining like terms and expanding or factoring with whole number coefficients, and only then return to the negative and fractional coefficients this standard demands.

steps.rationale: The lowest-band engine task is finding a missing coefficient by adding two linear expressions. Collecting like terms -- x-terms together, constants together, every sign carried -- is the commutative/associative property in action and the first way the standard creates an equivalent expression.

The standard explicitly says 'justify each step.' Before a student can justify their own work, they must be able to look at a single equivalence step and name the property (commutative, associative, distributive, identity) that makes it legal.

The At-proficiency core: apply the distributive property to expand a rational coefficient over a parenthesis and then combine like terms. The hard cases -- negative and fractional coefficients -- are the real difficulty and must be reliable before they can be one step inside a bigger problem.

The standard names factoring out a common number explicitly, with its own worked example (2x - 10 = 2(x - 5)). Factoring is distribution reversed: pull the greatest common factor to write p(qx + r), the exact form the content limits require.

The full At-proficiency demand: simplify a multi-part expression using several operations at once (distribute, subtract a group, combine) and justify each step -- and, by extension, find the first error in someone else's multi-step work. This is where an early sign slip corrupts the whole result.

The Above-proficiency payoff: generate MULTIPLE equivalent expressions from one, and prove equivalence. Substitution becomes the certifying tool -- two forms are equivalent only if they give the same value for every input.

skills.name: Break apart a multiplication fact with an area model

prerequisite_skill.description: Split one factor by place value and multiply each part, using a rectangle cut into two rooms to show why both parts get multiplied.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: How can you break apart 6 x 14 into two easier products?

skills.i_do_script: A hard fact breaks into two easy ones, and a rectangle shows why. Watch: 6 x 14. I draw a rectangle 6 tall and 14 wide, then cut the 14 into 10 and 4. The left room is 6 by 10, area 60. The right room is 6 by 4, area 24. The whole rectangle is 60 + 24 = 84, so 6 x 14 = 6 x 10 + 6 x 4. The 6 has to multiply BOTH parts, because the 6 is the height of both rooms. If I only multiplied one room, I would be leaving part of the rectangle uncounted.

canonical_error.pattern: Multiplies only one part of the split factor and adds the other part unchanged
canonical_error.example: Writes 6 x 14 = 6 x 10 + 4 = 64 instead of 6 x 10 + 6 x 4 = 84
canonical_error.why: The student splits 14 into 10 and 4 but lets the 6 reach only the 10. In the rectangle, the 6 is the height of both rooms, so both the 10 and the 4 must be multiplied by 6.

skills.item_template: A one-digit by two-digit fact. Student splits the two-digit factor by place value, names the two partial products from an area model, or computes the total. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: Fill in the blank: 6 x 14 = 6 x 10 + 6 x __
A rectangle is 6 tall and 14 wide, cut into a 6 by 10 room and a 6 by 4 room. What are the two areas?
Use breaking apart to find 4 x 13.
Use breaking apart to find 7 x 12.
5 x 16 = 5 x 10 + 5 x 6. What is 5 x 16?
Use breaking apart to find 3 x 24.
Which breaks apart 9 x 12 correctly: 9 x 10 + 9 x 2, or 9 x 10 + 2?
sample_items.answer: 9 x 10 + 9 x 2, because the 9 must multiply both parts

sample_items.stem: Use breaking apart to find 8 x 15.

redirect_script.stop: Did the outside number multiply BOTH parts?
redirect_script.prompt: Draw the rectangle and cut it into two rooms. The height touches both rooms, so it multiplies both widths. Say both products out loud before you add.
redirect_script.praise: You multiplied both rooms and added, that is exactly how breaking apart works.

vocabulary.definition: A rectangle whose area shows a multiplication; cutting it into rooms shows a fact breaking into parts.
The area of one room, like the 60 and the 24 inside 6 x 14.

next_steps.if_fail: Review grade 3 multiplication with equal groups and arrays (rows and columns of dots).

worked_example_script.text: Draw a rectangle 6 tall and 14 wide. Cut the width into 10 and 4 so there are two rooms.
What is the area of the left room? What is the area of the right room?
Left room: 6 x 10 = 60. Right room: 6 x 4 = 24. The whole rectangle is 60 + 24 = 84, so 6 x 14 = 84. The 6 multiplied both parts because it is the height of both rooms.
If a student writes 6 x 10 + 4, point at the right room: is its area really just 4? Who multiplies its width?
Your turn: draw the rectangle for 4 x 13 and find the two areas.

skills.name: Read phrases and parentheses to tell what to compute first

prerequisite_skill.description: Match a phrase like 'the sum of' to its operation and use parentheses to do the grouped part of a numerical expression first.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: In 3 x (4 + 2), what do you compute first, and what is the answer?

skills.i_do_script: An expression is a set of instructions, and parentheses tell me which instruction comes first. Watch: 3 x (4 + 2). The parentheses wrap the sum, so I add first: 4 + 2 = 6. Then I multiply: 3 x 6 = 18. Without the parentheses, 3 x 4 + 2 means multiply first, giving 12 + 2 = 14. Those are different answers, so the parentheses matter. Phrases work the same way: 'the sum of 4 and 2' means 4 + 2, 'the product of 3 and 5' means 3 x 5, and 'three times the sum of 4 and 2' means the sum is wrapped up first, 3 x (4 + 2).

canonical_error.pattern: Ignores the parentheses and computes left to right, or matches a phrase to the wrong operation
canonical_error.example: Computes 2 x (5 + 1) as 2 x 5 + 1 = 11 instead of 2 x 6 = 12
canonical_error.why: The student treats the parentheses as decoration instead of as a package that must be finished first. The grouped part is one quantity, and the outside number acts on all of it.

skills.item_template: A numerical expression with one set of parentheses, or a phrase to translate. Student names the first step, computes the value, or writes the expression. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: Which operation does 'the sum of 8 and 5' describe?
In 3 x (4 + 2), what do you compute first?
sample_items.answer: 4 + 2, because it is inside the parentheses

sample_items.stem: Write 'add 7 and 3, then multiply the result by 2' as an expression.
Do 2 x (5 + 1) and 2 x 5 + 1 have the same value?
Which phrase matches 6 x (2 + 9): 'six times two, plus nine' or 'six times the sum of two and nine'?
sample_items.answer: Six times the sum of two and nine

redirect_script.stop: What is wrapped inside the parentheses?
redirect_script.prompt: Finish the package first: compute what is inside the parentheses and replace it with one number. Then do the outside operation on that whole number.
redirect_script.praise: You finished the grouped part first, that is exactly what the parentheses ask for.

vocabulary.definition: Grouping symbols that wrap part of an expression; the wrapped part is computed first.
The result of adding, so 'the sum of 4 and 2' means 4 + 2.
The result of multiplying, so 'the product of 3 and 5' means 3 x 5.

next_steps.if_fail: Review grade 4 comparison and operation vocabulary with matching cards (phrase to number sentence).

worked_example_script.text: Write 3 x (4 + 2) and 3 x 4 + 2 side by side. Under the first, draw a box around (4 + 2) like a wrapped package.
In the boxed one, what has to happen before the 3 can multiply anything?
The package is finished first: 4 + 2 = 6, then 3 x 6 = 18. In the unboxed one we multiply first: 12 + 2 = 14. Different answers, so the parentheses change the meaning.
If a student gets 14 for the boxed one, redraw the box and ask what is inside it.
Your turn: compute (10 - 4) x 5, and say which step you did first.

skills.name: Combine like terms with whole number coefficients

prerequisite_skill.description: Simplify an expression like 4x + 2 + 3x by adding the x-terms together and keeping the plain number separate.

skills.i_do_script: Picture x as a sealed bag holding a number nobody knows. Then 4x + 2 + 3x is 4 bags, 2 loose counters, and 3 more bags. Bags pile with bags: 4 + 3 = 7, so 7x. The 2 loose counters stay their own pile, because a counter is not a bag. The simplified expression is 7x + 2. One warning: a plain x is 1 bag, so 5y + y is 5 + 1 = 6 bags, 6y. And 6x + 5 can never become 11x, because 5 counters are not 5 bags.

canonical_error.pattern: Combines a variable term with a plain number, or drops the invisible coefficient 1
canonical_error.why: The student adds every number in sight instead of sorting by kind. An x-term and a plain number are different kinds of pieces and stay separate, and a bare y counts as 1y.

skills.item_template: An expression with two or three variable terms and up to two constants, all whole number coefficients, no negatives. Student simplifies or names the like terms. Short response.

sample_items.stem: Which terms in 5x + 4 + 2x are like terms?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Like terms share the same variable part. Picking 5x and 4, or all three, means the student is grouping by 'they are numbers' instead of by variable part.

sample_items.answer: No. 6x has a variable and 5 does not, so they are not like terms and stay separate.

redirect_script.stop: Are those two pieces the same kind of thing?
redirect_script.prompt: Sort first: bags of x in one pile, loose counters in another. Only pieces of the same kind combine, and a bare x counts as 1 bag.
redirect_script.praise: You sorted by kind before you added, that is what combining like terms means.

vocabulary.definition: Terms with the exact same variable part, like 4x and 2x.
The number multiplying the variable, like the 4 in 4x; a bare x has coefficient 1.
A plain number with no variable, like the 2 in 4x + 2.

worked_example_script.text: Draw 4x + 2 + 3x as stuff on a table: 4 bags labeled x, 2 loose counters, 3 more bags labeled x.
Push the bags together. How many bags? Do the counters join the bag pile?
4 bags and 3 bags make 7 bags: 7x. The 2 counters stay a separate pile. The simplified expression is 7x + 2.
If a student writes 9x, ask which pile the 2 counters went into and whether counters are bags.
Your turn: simplify 6a + 3 + 2a + 4.

practice_problems.stem: Write an expression with four terms that simplifies to 5x + 7.
Mia simplified 6x + 5 + 2x and wrote 13x. Find her mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: She combined the constant 5 with the x-terms. Only 6x and 2x are like terms: 6x + 2x = 8x, and the 5 stays separate. Correct answer: 8x + 5.

activities.title: Bags and Counters
activities.instructions:
1. Build 4x + 2 + 3x on the table: 4 bags, 2 counters, 3 bags.
2. Push same-kind pieces into piles: bags with bags, counters with counters.
3. Write the expression for what is on the table now: 7x + 2.
4. Repeat with 6a + 3 + 2a + 4 and 5y + y (use one bag alone to show 1y).
5. Say each time: bags pile with bags, counters pile with counters.

activities.title: Like or Not
activities.instructions:
1. Each card shows two terms, like '4x and 2x' or '3x and 7'.
2. Sort the card into 'Like terms' or 'Not like terms'.
3. Rule to place a card: if they are alike, say their combined value out loud; if not, say why in one sentence.
4. Debrief: which cards tricked people into adding a number to an x-term?

strategy_links.why: Bags and counters make 'only same-kind pieces combine' visible before any rule about like terms is named.
The 6x + 5 = 11x error is precise and predictable, ideal for a find-and-fix routine.
Choral response on 'bags with bags, counters with counters' hard-wires the sorting habit.

questioning_prompts: Which terms here are the same kind of piece?
What is the coefficient of a bare x or y?
Why can 6x and 5 never combine into one term?
What do the x-terms add to? What do the plain numbers add to?
How could you check your answer by substituting x = 2?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student adds a constant into the x-term total, like 6x + 5 + 2x = 13x.
misconception_redirects.say: Point at the table: are the 5 counters bags? Sort into piles first, then add each pile separately.
misconception_redirects.praise: You kept the piles separate, so every piece landed where it belongs.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student treats a bare y as zero y or drops it, like 5y + y = 5y.
misconception_redirects.say: A bag standing alone is still 1 bag. Write the invisible 1: y means 1y, so 5 + 1 = 6.
misconception_redirects.praise: You counted the lone bag as 1, that is what the invisible coefficient means.

quick_checks.look_for: 8x + 4. An answer of 12x means the constant was folded into the x-terms.
8y + 2. An answer of 7y + 2 means the bare y was not counted as 1y.

steps.annotation: Bags of a in one pile, plain numbers in another.
Add the coefficients of the like terms.
Add the constants in their own pile.
One a-term and one constant, fully combined.
x-terms together, the constant on its own.
Add the coefficients 4 and 3.
Decide what happens to the 2.
Write the simplified expression.

The ___ stays separate because it has no variable.

skills.name: Expand and factor expressions with whole number coefficients

prerequisite_skill.description: Use the distributive property to expand an expression like 3(x + 4) and to factor one like 6x + 9, with whole numbers only.

skills.i_do_script: This is the grade 4 rectangle again, with a bag inside. Watch: 3(x + 4) is a rectangle 3 tall whose width is x + 4. Cut it into two rooms: one 3 by x, area 3x, and one 3 by 4, area 12. So 3(x + 4) = 3x + 12. The 3 multiplies BOTH terms because it is the height of both rooms. Factoring runs the same picture backwards: for 6x + 9, the biggest number dividing both 6 and 9 is 3, so the height is 3. The widths are 6x divided by 3, which is 2x, and 9 divided by 3, which is 3. So 6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3). I always check by expanding back: 3 times 2x is 6x, 3 times 3 is 9. It matches.

canonical_error.pattern: Distributes to the first term only, or factors without dividing every term
canonical_error.why: The student lets the outside number reach only the first room of the rectangle. Expanding must multiply every term inside, and factoring must divide every term by the common factor, or the two forms stop being equal.

skills.item_template: Expand p(qx + r) or factor ax + b using the greatest common factor. Whole number coefficients only, no negatives. Short response or multiple choice.

sample_items.distractor_logic: 2 must multiply both terms: 2x and 10. Choosing 2x + 5 means the 2 reached only the x; x + 10 means it reached only the 5.

redirect_script.stop: Did the outside number reach BOTH rooms?
redirect_script.prompt: Draw the rectangle: the outside number is the height of both rooms, so it multiplies both terms. When factoring, divide EVERY term by the common factor, then expand back to check.
redirect_script.praise: You multiplied both terms and checked by expanding, that keeps the two forms equal.

vocabulary.definition: A number outside parentheses multiplies each term inside: a(b + c) = ab + ac.
To write an expression as a number times a parenthesis, like 6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3).
The largest number that divides evenly into every term, like 3 for 6x and 9.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a rectangle 3 tall. Cut its width into x and 4, making a 3 by x room and a 3 by 4 room.
What is the area of each room? What is the total area?
The rooms have areas 3x and 12, so 3(x + 4) = 3x + 12. This is the same break-apart picture as 6 x 14, just with a bag of x as one width.
If a student writes 3x + 4, point at the second room: with height 3 and width 4, can its area be 4?
Now run it backwards: for 6x + 9, what height divides both areas, and what are the two widths?

practice_problems.stem: What is the greatest common factor of 6 and 9?
Factor 12x + 18 completely, then expand to check.
practice_problems.answer: 6(2x + 3); check: 6 times 2x = 12x and 6 times 3 = 18. Factoring out only 2 or 3 leaves a common factor inside.

practice_problems.stem: Leo expanded 3(x + 4) and wrote 3x + 4. Find his mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: The 3 multiplied the x but never reached the 4. It must multiply both terms: 3 times 4 = 12, so 3(x + 4) = 3x + 12.

activities.title: Rooms and Widths
materials: Index card labeled x for the unknown width
activities.instructions:
1. Build 3(x + 4) on grid paper: a rectangle 3 tall, with an x-card for one width and 4 squares for the other.
2. Write each room's area inside it: 3x and 12. Record 3(x + 4) = 3x + 12.
3. Now go backwards: given 6x + 9, find the height that divides both areas (3) and label the widths 2x and 3.
4. Repeat with 5(2x + 3) forwards and 8x + 12 backwards.
5. Say each time: the height multiplies every width.

activities.title: Expand and Factor Match-Up
materials: Card deck: factored-form cards and expanded-form cards, plus two decoys
activities.instructions:
1. Spread all cards face up.
2. Match each factored form like 3(x + 4) to its expanded twin like 3x + 12.
3. Two expanded cards are decoys where the outside number missed a term; set them aside and name the missing product.
4. To claim a match, say both products out loud.

strategy_links.why: The area model makes 'the outside number multiplies every term' concrete, and links straight back to the grade 4 break-apart rectangle.
The missed-term expansion 3x + 4 is a stable, baitable error that a find-and-fix routine confronts directly.
Placing 3(2x + 3) next to the wrong 3(2x + 9) and expanding both makes 'divide every term' explicit through contrast.

questioning_prompts: How many terms are inside? So how many products should you get?
What is the height of the rectangle, and which widths does it multiply?
What is the greatest number that divides every term?
If you expand your factored form, do you get back the original?
Is there still a common factor left inside the parentheses?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student expands to the first term only, like 3(x + 4) = 3x + 4.
misconception_redirects.say: Draw the rectangle: the 3 is the height of BOTH rooms. What is 3 times 4? Both products go in the answer.
misconception_redirects.praise: You multiplied both terms, so the expansion matches the rectangle.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student factors without dividing every term, like 6x + 9 = 3(2x + 9).
misconception_redirects.say: Expand your answer back: 3 times 9 is 27, not 9. Divide the 9 by 3 too, then check again.
misconception_redirects.praise: You divided every term and checked by expanding, that is a true factoring.

quick_checks.look_for: 4x + 8. An answer of 4x + 2 means the 4 never reached the 2.
5(2x + 3). An answer of 5(2x + 15) or 5(x + 3) means a term was not divided correctly.

steps.annotation: The 5 is the height of both rooms.
Area of the first room.
Area of the second room, the 5 reaches it too.
Total area, both products included.

steps.math: draw: rectangle 4 tall, widths x and 6
steps.annotation: Two rooms, one height.
Area of the first room.
Find the area of the second room: 4 times 6.
Write the expanded expression with both products.

sentence_starters: The outside number ___ multiplies both ___ and ___.
The greatest common factor is ___, so the factored form is ___.
I checked by expanding back and got ___.

skills.name: Combine like terms to create an equivalent linear expression
skills.i_do_script: Think of -y as one bag of y you OWE, not one you own -- an owed bag cancels one of your real bags. Put the piles on the table first and the count comes out on its own. To create an equivalent expression by adding or subtracting, I combine like terms: x-terms with x-terms, numbers with numbers, and I keep every sign. Watch: (-y + 5) + (7y - 9). The y-terms are -1y and 7y; -1 + 7 = 6, so 6y. The numbers are 5 and -9; 5 - 9 = -4. So the equivalent expression is 6y - 4. The number stuck to the first y is -1, not 1 -- dropping that negative is the classic mistake.

canonical_error.pattern: Drops the negative on a variable term (or combines a variable term with a constant) when collecting like terms
canonical_error.example: For (-y + 5) + (7y - 9) the student treats -y as +y, computing 1 + 7 = 8 and reporting 8y instead of 6y
canonical_error.why: The student reads the coefficient of -y as 1 rather than -1, so the sign is lost before the terms are added. Every term carries the sign directly in front of it, and that sign must travel with the coefficient when like terms are combined.

skills.item_template: Two linear binomials added, with one coefficient unknown (n*var + b), or a two-expression sum to simplify. Integer or simple rational coefficients; one variable. Short numeric/expression response.

sample_items.stem: Enter the value of n so that (-y + 5) + (7y - 9) is equivalent to (ny - 4).
sample_items.distractor_logic: -1 + 7 = 6. Reading -y as +y gives the trap answer 8; combining the constants into the coefficient gives other wrong values.
2 + 5 = 7 and 6 - 1 = 5. Adding 6 + 1 or 2 + 5 + 6 - 1 into one number are the common slips.
3 + (-6) = -3 and 2 + 3 = 5. Reading -6x as +6x gives 9x, the sign-drop error.

sample_items.stem: Enter the value of n so that (4x - 7) + (-9x + 2) is equivalent to (nx - 5).
sample_items.distractor_logic: 4 + (-9) = -5; the constants -7 + 2 = -5 confirm the form. Dropping the negative on -9x gives +13 or +5.

redirect_script.stop: Wait -- what sign is in front of that term?
redirect_script.prompt: Look back at the piles: is that first bag one you own or one you OWE? Write the sign directly on the coefficient: -y means -1y. Then add the variable terms in one pile and the numbers in another, carrying every sign.
redirect_script.praise: You carried the negative with the term -- that's how like terms really combine.

vocabulary.definition: Terms with the exact same variable part, so their coefficients can be added.
Two expressions that give the same value for every value of the variable.
The rational number multiplied by a variable, like the -1 in -y or the 7 in 7y.

worked_example_script.text: Sketch (-y + 5) + (7y - 9) as piles: 1 bag of y OWED and 5 counters, next to 7 bags of y and 9 counters OWED.
Push all the bags together: you hold 7 bags but owe 1 -- how many bags are really yours? Now the counters: you hold 5 but owe 9 -- where does that leave you?

The owed bag cancels one of the 7, leaving 6 bags; 5 counters against 9 owed leaves 4 owed. That is 6y - 4. Counting 8 bags means you counted the OWED bag as one you own -- the pile picture catches it instantly.
Which terms have a y? What is the sign in front of the first y?
The y-terms are -1y and 7y: -1 + 7 = 6, so 6y. The numbers are 5 and -9: 5 - 9 = -4. Result: 6y - 4.
If the student writes 8y, stop and ask 'is the first term +y or -y?'
Your turn: (3x + 2) + (-6x + 3).

practice_problems.stem: Enter the value of n so that (-y + 5) + (7y - 9) is equivalent to (ny - 4).
practice_problems.notes: Spec Below item; baits reading -y as +y.
Straight combine, positive coefficients.

practice_problems.stem: Riley combined the like terms in (-y + 5) + (7y - 9). Find and fix the mistake.
practice_problems.answer: Riley dropped the negative on the first y. It is -1y, so -1 + 7 = 6, not 8. The correct equivalent expression is 6y - 4.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: sign lost on a leading -y term.
Negative x-coefficient in the second group.

practice_problems.stem: Enter the value of n so that (4x - 7) + (-9x + 2) is equivalent to (nx - 5).
practice_problems.notes: Both coefficient and constant land on -5 -- must keep them separate.

practice_problems.stem: Write two binomials whose sum is 5x - 3, then check by combining.
practice_problems.notes: Reversed direction -- build a pair with a known sum.

4. Rule to place a card: if they are alike, write their combined value; if not, say why in one word.

materials: Slip with Riley's combine ending in 8y - 4
activities.instructions:

2. Circle the exact spot where the negative on -y disappeared.
3. Redo the y-terms with the sign carried, and write the correct answer.
4. Write the one rule that prevents this error every time.

skills.name: Identify the property of operations that justifies a step
skills.i_do_script: Justifying a step means naming the property that makes it legal. The four we use: commutative (change the ORDER, like 3 + x = x + 3), associative (change the GROUPING, like (2 + x) + 5 = 2 + (x + 5)), distributive (a number outside parentheses multiplies each term inside, like 3(x + 2) = 3x + 6), and identity (adding 0 or multiplying by 1 changes nothing). Watch: 5(x + 3) = 5x + 15 -- the 5 reached both terms inside, so that is the distributive property, not commutative.

canonical_error.pattern: Confuses the distributive property with commutative/associative, or swaps commutative (order) and associative (grouping)
canonical_error.example: Labels 3(x + 2) = 3x + 6 as the commutative property because the terms look rearranged, when multiplying across the parentheses is the distributive property
canonical_error.why: The student matches by surface appearance instead of what actually changed. Distributive means a number multiplied every term inside parentheses; commutative means only the order changed; associative means only the grouping (parentheses) moved.

skills.item_template: A single equivalence step shown; student selects the property (commutative, associative, distributive, identity) that justifies it. Integer coefficients. Multiple choice.

sample_items.distractor_logic: A number multiplied each term inside the parentheses -- that is distribution. The rearranged look tempts 'commutative.'
Only the grouping (parentheses) moved; order and values stayed -- that is associative, not commutative.
Only the order of the two terms flipped -- commutative. No grouping changed and nothing was distributed.

sample_items.stem: Which property is demonstrated? x + 0 = x
sample_items.distractor_logic: Adding 0 leaves the value unchanged -- the additive identity. Inverse would be x + (-x) = 0.

redirect_script.stop: What actually changed from the left side to the right?
redirect_script.prompt: Ask one question: did a number get multiplied into a parenthesis (distributive), did only the ORDER flip (commutative), or did only the GROUPING move (associative)? Point to the exact change.
redirect_script.praise: You named the property by what changed, not by how it looks -- that's real justification.

vocabulary.definition: You can change the order of terms in addition or multiplication: a + b = b + a.
You can change the grouping (the parentheses) without changing the value: (a + b) + c = a + (b + c).
A number outside parentheses multiplies each term inside: a(b + c) = ab + ac.
Adding 0 or multiplying by 1 leaves a number unchanged: x + 0 = x.

worked_example_script.text: What did the 5 do to get to the right side?
The 5 multiplied each term inside the parentheses: 5 times x is 5x, 5 times 3 is 15. A number multiplying each term inside is the distributive property.
If the student says 'commutative,' ask 'did only the ORDER change, or did a number multiply into the parentheses?'
Your turn: name the property in (2 + x) + 5 = 2 + (x + 5).

practice_problems.stem: What does the distributive property let you do to a(b + c)?

practice_problems.notes: Spec-style; baits 'commutative.'

practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: calling distribution 'commutative' by surface look.

skills.name: Distribute a rational coefficient and combine like terms
skills.i_do_script: Before any rule, let a pattern set the signs: multiplying 3x - 7 by 2, then 1, then 0 steps the answer down by 3x and UP by 7 each time -- and nothing stops that ladder at zero. Distributing means the number outside the parentheses multiplies EVERY term inside, and the signs come along. Watch a tricky one: -4(3x - 7). The -4 hits 3x: -4 times 3 is -12, so -12x. The -4 hits -7: negative times negative is POSITIVE, so +28. The result is -12x + 28. After distributing I combine any like terms -- for 5x + (1/2)(4x - 8), I distribute to get 2x - 4, then 5x + 2x = 7x, giving 7x - 4.

canonical_error.pattern: Distributes to the first term only, or keeps the wrong sign on the second product (misses that negative times negative is positive)
canonical_error.example: For -4(3x - 7) the student writes -12x - 28, keeping the minus instead of computing -4 times -7 = +28
canonical_error.why: The student applies the outside number's sign to the operation instead of computing a signed product, or treats the parenthesis as attached only to the leading term. Both terms must be multiplied, and negative times negative is positive.

skills.item_template: An expression p(qx + r) with a rational p (negative or fractional), optionally added to a loose like term. Student distributes and combines. Integer, decimal, or fraction coefficients. Short response.

sample_items.stem: Use the distributive property to simplify: -4(3x - 7).
sample_items.distractor_logic: -4 times 3x = -12x; -4 times -7 = +28. '-12x - 28' keeps the minus (misses negative times negative).
(1/2)(4x - 8) = 2x - 4, then 5x + 2x = 7x. Forgetting to multiply the -8 by 1/2 leaves 5x + 2x - 8.
-0.8 times (10.8x + 3.2x = 14x) = -11.2x; -0.8 times -20 = +16. Missing the +16 sign or not combining the x-terms yields the distractors.
3 times 2x = 6x; 3 times 5 = 15. '6x + 5' skips the second product.

redirect_script.stop: Did the outside number reach the SECOND term too?
redirect_script.prompt: Check the ladder first: as the outside number steps below zero, which way is the constant moving? Draw an arrow from the outside number to each term inside and say the product out loud with its sign: 'negative four times negative seven is positive twenty-eight.' Then combine like terms.
redirect_script.praise: You multiplied both terms and kept the signs straight -- clean distribution.

vocabulary.definition: A number outside parentheses multiplies each term inside: a(b + c) = ab + ac.
A single number or variable piece separated by + or -, like the 3x and the -7 in 3x - 7.
The rational number multiplied by a variable, like the -4 in -4(3x - 7) or the 1/2 in (1/2)(4x - 8).

worked_example_script.text: Each step down, the x-part drops by 3x and the number CLIMBS by 7. Keep stepping below zero: -1(3x - 7) = ? Then -2, -3, all the way to -4(3x - 7) = ?
The ladder forces -3x + 7, then -6x + 14, -9x + 21, and -12x + 28. The constant keeps climbing into the positives, so -4(3x - 7) MUST end in +28 -- writing -28 breaks a pattern you can see.
How many terms are inside? So how many products will we get?
Two terms, two products. -4 times 3x is -12x. -4 times -7 is +28 -- negative times negative is positive. Result: -12x + 28.
If the student writes -12x - 28, ask 'what is negative times negative?'
Your turn: 5x + (1/2)(4x - 8). Distribute, then combine.

skills.name: Factor out the greatest common number to write p(qx + r)
skills.i_do_script: Picture 36x + 9 as one rectangle with height 9, split into two rooms -- one room holds the area 36x, the other holds the area 9, and each room's width is what 9 must multiply to fill it. Factoring is distribution in reverse: I pull the greatest common factor out front and put what is left in parentheses. Watch: 36x + 9. The biggest number that divides both 36 and 9 is 9. I divide each term by 9: 36x divided by 9 is 4x, and 9 divided by 9 is 1. So 36x + 9 = 9(4x + 1). The standard's own example is 2x - 10 = 2(x - 5). I always check by distributing back: 9 times 4x is 36x, 9 times 1 is 9 -- it matches.

canonical_error.pattern: Pulls out a common factor but forgets to divide EVERY term by it (leaves a term unchanged), or uses a factor that isn't the greatest
canonical_error.example: For 36x + 9 the student writes 9(4x + 9), forgetting that 9 divided by 9 = 1, so the second term should be 1, not 9
canonical_error.why: The student divides the first term but copies the second term unchanged, breaking equivalence -- 9(4x + 9) expands to 36x + 81, not 36x + 9. Factoring only works if every term inside is the original term divided by the factor.

skills.item_template: A linear expression ax + b with a common factor; student writes p(qx + r) or p(qx - r) using the greatest common factor. Integer coefficients (a rational factor at the stretch). Multiple choice or short response.

sample_items.distractor_logic: GCF of 36 and 9 is 9: 36x/9 = 4x, 9/9 = 1. '9(4x + 9)'-style errors forget to divide the constant; 36(x + 1) = 36x + 36; 4(9x + 1) = 36x + 4.
GCF is 2: 2x/2 = x, -10/2 = -5. The standard's own example. Forgetting to divide -10 gives 2(x - 10).
GCF (with the negative pulled out) is -12: -72x/-12 = 6x, 60/-12 = -5. Sign errors on the constant give -12(6x + 5).

sample_items.stem: Factor: 15x - 25 using the greatest common factor.
sample_items.distractor_logic: GCF of 15 and 25 is 5: 15x/5 = 3x, -25/5 = -5. Using 3 or another non-greatest factor leaves a further common factor inside.

redirect_script.stop: Divide the constant by the factor too.
redirect_script.prompt: Go back to the rectangle: if the height is 9 and that room's area is only 9, how wide can the room be? After you pull out the factor, divide EACH term by it -- including the constant. Then distribute back to check: it must return the exact original expression.
redirect_script.praise: You divided every term by the factor and checked by distributing -- that's a valid factoring.

vocabulary.definition: A number that divides evenly into every term; to factor is to write the expression as that number times a parenthesis.
The largest number that divides evenly into all the terms, like 9 for 36x and 9.
The rule you use to check a factoring: p(qx + r) = pqx + pr should return the original.

worked_example_script.text: Draw one rectangle cut into two rooms. The left room has area 36x, the right room has area 9. Label the shared height 9 along the side.
With height 9, how wide is the left room -- 9 times what gives 36x? And the right room: 9 times WHAT gives an area of just 9?

The left width is 4x and the right width is 1, because 9 x 1 = 9. Total width 4x + 1, so the whole rectangle is 9(4x + 1). A width of 9 would make that little room's area 81 -- the picture will not allow it.
Write '36x + 9.'
What is the biggest number that divides both 36 and 9?
9 divides both. Divide each term by 9: 36x divided by 9 is 4x, and 9 divided by 9 is 1. So 36x + 9 = 9(4x + 1).
If the student writes 9(4x + 9), ask 'what is 9 divided by 9?'
Check by distributing back, then your turn: factor 2x - 10.

practice_problems.answer: Taylor forgot to divide the constant: 9 divided by 9 = 1, not 9. The correct factoring is 9(4x + 1). Check: 9(4x + 1) = 36x + 9, but 9(4x + 9) = 36x + 81.

skills.name: Simplify a multi-step expression and justify each step
skills.i_do_script: Subtracting a group means removing the WHOLE package -- and when the package is a debt, removing it makes you richer. Watch the debt slip get torn up before any rule is spoken. At this level I simplify multi-part expressions using several moves at once and justify each one, which also lets me spot where someone else went wrong. Watch: (2.1x + 4.3) - (-3x - 7). Subtracting a group flips every sign inside: -(-3x - 7) becomes +3x + 7. Now I combine: 2.1x + 3x = 5.1x and 4.3 + 7 = 11.3, so 5.1x + 11.3. The most common slip is in the arithmetic sign -- like doing 2.64 - 4.44 and writing 7.08 (adding) instead of -1.8 (subtracting).

canonical_error.pattern: Adds two constants instead of subtracting when one is negative (a sign slip in the final combine), or forgets that subtracting a group flips every sign inside
canonical_error.example: Simplifying 1.2(2.2 + 3y - 3.7), the student combines the constants 2.64 and -4.44 as 7.08 (adding) instead of -1.8 (subtracting), reporting 7.08 + 3.6y
canonical_error.why: The student ignores the sign of the -4.44 term and adds its absolute value, or drops the sign flip when a whole group is subtracted. Each constant keeps the sign in front of it, and subtracting a group distributes a -1 to every term inside.

skills.item_template: A multi-step simplification (distribute then combine, or subtract a group) shown as student work with one error, OR an expression to simplify with each step justified. Integer and decimal coefficients. DOK 3 multiple choice / short response.

sample_items.stem: A student simplified 1.2(2.2 + 3y - 3.7). Step 1: 1.2(2.2 + 3y - 3.7); Step 2: 2.64 + 3.6y - 4.44; Step 3: 2.64 - 4.44 + 3.6y; Step 4: 7.08 + 3.6y. In which step is the first error?
sample_items.answer: Step 4 -- 2.64 - 4.44 = -1.8, not 7.08 (the student added instead of subtracting).
choices: Step 3 -- the terms cannot be reordered.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Distribution and reordering are correct; the error is adding the constants instead of subtracting. Correct result: 3.6y - 1.8.
Subtracting the group flips signs: +3x + 7. Then 2.1x + 3x = 5.1x, 4.3 + 7 = 11.3. Keeping -3x - 7 gives -0.9x - 2.7.
-3 times -2 = +6, then 6 + 5 = 11. '-3x - 1' comes from making -3 times -2 negative.
3 - 6 = -3 and 2 + 3 = 5. Reading -6x as +6x gives 9x + 5.

redirect_script.stop: Check the sign on that constant before you combine.
redirect_script.prompt: See the group as one package first: what happens to each piece inside when the whole package is taken away? Rewrite each constant with its sign in front, then combine: 2.64 and -4.44 give 2.64 - 4.44 = -1.8. If a whole group is subtracted, flip every sign inside first.
redirect_script.praise: You tracked the sign through the combine -- that's why your justification holds.

vocabulary.definition: A number outside parentheses multiplies each term inside; subtracting a group is multiplying it by -1.
A number plus its opposite is 0; subtracting a term is adding its additive inverse.
A single number or variable piece separated by + or -, each carrying the sign in front of it.

worked_example_script.text: Picture (2.1x + 4.3) as your pile, and (-3x - 7) as a debt slip: 3 bags of x owed and 7 counters owed. Subtracting that group means someone tears up the debt slip.
When a debt of 3 bags and 7 counters disappears, is your pile bigger or smaller? By how many bags, and by how many counters?

Tearing up the debt makes you 3 bags and 7 counters RICHER: subtracting -3x - 7 adds +3x and +7. That is why every sign inside a subtracted group flips -- and why each constant must be combined with the sign it truly carries.
What happens to the signs inside the second group when we subtract it?
Subtracting flips every sign: -(-3x - 7) becomes +3x + 7. Now combine: 2.1x + 3x = 5.1x and 4.3 + 7 = 11.3. Result: 5.1x + 11.3.
If a student keeps -3x - 7, ask 'what does the minus in front of the parenthesis do to each term?'
Your turn: -3(x - 2) + 5. Distribute, then combine -- watch the signs.

practice_problems.answer: The first error is in Step 4: the student added 4.44 to 2.64 instead of subtracting. 2.64 - 4.44 = -1.8, so the correct result is 3.6y - 1.8.

skills.name: Create and verify multiple equivalent expressions
skills.i_do_script: At the top level I create MULTIPLE equivalent expressions from one, and I can prove two forms are equal. Watch: 6x + 3(2x + 3) + 8x. Distribute the 3: 6x + 6x + 9 + 8x -- that is already one equivalent form, 12x + 9 + 8x. Combine all the x-terms: 6 + 6 + 8 = 20, so the fully simplified form is 20x + 9. To prove two forms match, I substitute a value: at x = 1 the original is 6 + 15 + 8 = 29, and 20x + 9 is 29 -- equal.

canonical_error.pattern: Produces a form that is not actually equivalent -- a sign slip when subtracting a group or a missed term -- instead of a genuinely equal expression
canonical_error.example: For 3x + 5(-4x + 12) - (x - 3) the student writes -x - 3 for the last group (should be -x + 3), reporting -18x + 57 instead of -18x + 63
canonical_error.why: The student treats 'equivalent' as 'looks similar' and skips the substitution check that would catch the error. Two expressions are equivalent only if they give the same value for every input, which a single sign slip destroys.

activities.title: Equivalent Expression Chains
activities.instructions:
1. Draw a start card (like 6x + 3(2x + 3) + 8x).
2. Write three DIFFERENT equivalent forms in the blanks: one after distributing, one partially combined, one fully simplified.
3. Pick x = 2 and evaluate the start card and all three forms -- every value must match.
4. Trade strips; a partner accepts your chain only if all four values are equal.
5. Debrief: how did substitution catch any form that was not really equivalent?

activities.title: Is It Really Equivalent?
activities.instructions:
1. Read Jordan's simplification of 3x + 5(-4x + 12) - (x - 3) ending in -18x + 57.
2. Substitute x = 1 into the original and into -18x + 57 -- do they match?
3. Find the dropped sign and rewrite the correct equivalent form.
4. Write the rule: what does subtracting a group do to every sign inside?

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S3, distributing a rational coefficient and combining like terms, the At-proficiency core. If they pass, push to S5 (multi-step simplification with justification) and S6 (create and verify multiple equivalent forms). If they fail, drop below grade level: B1 checks combining like terms with whole number coefficients and B2 checks expanding and factoring with whole numbers, the grade 6 versions of the standard's two engines. S1, S2, and S4 remain available to probe signed combining, property naming, and factoring on grade level.
